49/S0.subgoal: Explain the two perspectives of optimization in immersive VR—psychophysiological experience and technological resource utilization—their trade-off, and that the lecture focuses on experience optimization.

49/S1.subgoal: Explain what cybersickness is, its internal and external causes, and why mitigation strategies must avoid compromising presence.

49/S2.subgoal: Describe VR locomotion techniques and user- versus system-controlled virtual tours, and relate them to reducing navigation duration or distance to minimize cybersickness.

49/S3.subgoal: Explain why the lecture focuses on realistic walking in system-controlled tours and why optic flow must match the user's instantaneous walking speed, motivating a walking-speed model.

49/S4.subgoal: Summarize the main points of the lecture.

goal.goal: Explain how VR experience optimization is guided by cybersickness and presence constraints, from the trade-off with resource utilization through locomotion choices to the need for walking-speed-matched optic flow in system-controlled tours.
goal.achieves: This supports the course aim of addressing psycho-physiological issues and optimization from user and developer perspectives, preparing the learner to understand and evaluate immersive XR experience design.

objectives.goal: Explain why immersive VR optimization should prioritize psychophysiological experience over technological resource utilization by identifying cybersickness causes and the presence constraints on mitigation.
objectives.achieves: This helps the learner understand the user-centric aim of VR optimization and the comfort and presence constraints that mitigation strategies must satisfy.

objectives.goal: Describe how VR locomotion and user- and system-controlled tour choices can reduce cybersickness through shorter navigation duration or distance, and why system-controlled tours require realistic walking with optic flow matched to the user's instantaneous speed.
objectives.achieves: This lets the learner identify the movement-design problem in VR tours and understand why a walking-speed model is needed to keep optic flow realistic and comfortable.
